September 4, 1924 
With the view of promoting health and efficiency and of minimizing accidents among Federal employees, the heads of the several executive departments and independent establishments having a medical personnel are directed to make such physical examinations of applicants for and employees in the Federal classified service as may be requested by the Civil Service Commission or its authorized 
representatives. This order will supplement the Executive orders of May 29 and June 18, 1923. 
ORDERS EXCEPTING PERSONS NAMED FROM THE REQUIRE- MENTS OF THE RULES . 
August 17, 1923 
Hon. David W. Davis, who has been serving temporarily as Commissioner of the Reclamation Service, may be permanently appointed to that position without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. 
November 3, 1923 
Mrs. Lyne Pepper Smith, widow of Col. Thomas L. Smith, may be appointed to a clerical position in the War Department without reference to the civil- service rules. This order is issued for charitable purposes upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that Colonel Smith’s death, which occurred October 31, 1922, was hastened by his devotion to duty and his arduous labor during the World War. He was commissioned a second lieutenant in the Army: in June, 1893, and was examined for promotion to lieutenant colonel but was found physically incapacitated for active service, because of disability incurred in line of duty, and was retired December 5, 1915. He was one of the first retired officers to request assignment to active duty at the outbreak of the World War. He served until March 11, 1922, when he was again placed on the retired list as colonel.

TRANSFER OF RECORDS OF THE UNITED STATES FOOD ADMINISTRATION 
April 17, 1924 
Whereas, by virtue of an Executive order, dated August 21, 1920, all records and certain filing equipment of the cereal enforcement division of the United States Food Administration were transferred to the Treasury Department of the United States for safe keeping, and, later, by the provisions of the budget and accounting act of June 10, 1921, transferred to the Comptroller General of the United States; and Whereas it is desirable that all records of the United States Food Adminis- tration be kept together, all other records of the United States Food Adminis- tration being now in the custody of the United States Grain Corporation by virtue of the same Executive order: I hereby order and direct that all the records and all equipment transferred and delivered as aforesaid and now in the custody of the Comptroller General of the United States be transferred and delivered to the United States Grain Corporation and preserved in its custody until the further order of the President.

Bureau of Labor Statistics, on March 19, 1918, since which time he has been
engaged in work similar to that required in the position to be filled and has had
constant contact with the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement of Mr. Hanna
which is desired by the department as in the interests of the service.
February 4, 1926.
Mrs. Mabel A. Murphy may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been
_separated from the service.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the
Treasury, who states that her husband, formerly employed by the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing, has made application for retirement on account of total
disability and leaves Mrs. Murphy with two daughters to support with no
resources to speak of. She was employed in the Bureau of Engraving and
Printing and the office of the Treasurer of the United States from July 13,
1899, to November 7, 1907.
As the Civil Service Commission can properly recommend waivers only when
the procedure under the rules will not fully meet the needs of the service, it is
unable to concur.
Done for charity.
February 5, 1926.
Mrs. Stella Davis Mudd may be reinstated as telephone switchboard operator
in the naval powder factory at Indianhead, Md., without regard to the length of

EXCEPTION OF THREE EXPERTS AND FIVE MEMBERS OF A BOARD OF ENGINEERS, 
INTERSTATE COMMERCE COMMISSION. April 23, 1913. 
Schedule A of the civil-service rules specifying classified positions which may be filled without examination or upon noncompetitive examination is hereby amended by adding at the end thereof a new subdivision to be numbered XII, as follows: 
XII. INTERSTATE COMMERCE COMMISSION. 
1. Three experts to be members of an advisory board under the act of March 1, 1913, providing for the valuation of the property of carriers. 2. Five members of a board of engineers under said act. 
RESTORATION OF CHIEF POST-OFFICE INSPECTOR TO COMPETITIVE CLASS. 
May 7, 1913. 
The list of classified positions excepted from examination under civil-service Rule 11, clause 3, is hereby amended so as to omit the position of chief post-office inspector in the Post Office Department. 
The effect of the above order was to restore the position of post-office inspector to the competitive class. The position was transferred from the excepted to the com- petitive class by the revision of the rules on May 6, 1896. It was placed in the excepted class by the order of January 4, 1910. 
EXCEPTING ONE PRIVATE SECRETARY TO EACH HEAD OF BUREAU NOT CONFIRMED BY THE SENATE. June 6, 1913. 
Schedule A, Subdivision I, peragraph 2 of the civil-service rules is hereby amended by striking out the words: ‘‘and confirmed by the Senate.” As amended clause 2 will read as follows: 
2. One private secretary or confidential clerk to each of the heads of bureaus appointed by the President in the executive departments, if authorized by law. 
This amendment is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce to permit appointment without examination of a ‘‘clerk to commissioner,”” Bureau of Corporations, a position authorized by law, and is concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. The Commissioner of Corporations is appointed by the President without confir- mation, and he was not therefore entitled to the exception from examination of a private secretary, a privilege limited to heads of bureaus appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. The amendment will obviate further recourse to the President in future similar cases. : 
EXCEPTION OF PRIVATE SECRETARY TO THE PUBLIC PRINTER. 
July 23, 1913. 
Schedule A, Subdivision I, paragraph 1 of the civil-service rules excepting posi- tions named from the requirement of examination is hereby amended by the addition of the following words: 
* * * and one to the Public Printer. 
As amended the exception contained in paragraph 1 will read as follows: 
1. Two private secretaries or confidential clerks to the head of each of the executive departments and one to each assistant head and one to the Public Printer. 
It was found necessary to permit the appointment of a private secretary to the Public Printer without examination by the Executive order of January 30, 1903, and again by the Executive order of June 9, 1908. The present amendment will permit the appointment of a new private secretary or confidential clerk as necessity arises without resort to a special Executive order and will also give the occupant of the position the status of an excepted rather than 
a competitive employee.

114 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
EXCEPTION OF ‘‘SPECIAL EMPLOYEES,’ 
August 2, 1913. 
Schedule A, Subdivision III, paragraph 14, of the civil-service rules, making exceptions from the requirement of examination in the Treasury Department, is amended to read as follows: 
14. Informers and posse men, and special employees employed temporarily for detective work in the Internal Revenue Service, under the appropriation for detecting and bringing to trial and punishment persons violating the internal-revenue laws. 
This amendment is made for the reason that the appropriation from which special employees are paid, ‘Punishment for violation of internal-revenue laws,”” contem- plates the, employment of special employees for purely detective work of a temporary character; that the personal services to be rendered are of a temporary, confidential, and secret character, and the classification of ‘‘special employees” by Executive order of August 24, 1912, has had the effect of defeating the object of the appropriation in that another class of permanent officers, generally known to the public, has been created who are performing duties similar to those of deputy collectors of internal revenue, but paid from the aforesaid appropriation, with the result that the payment of salaries of these permanent officers exhausts said appropriation to such an extent that the Commissioner of Internal Revenue is unable to employ the necessary detective force to prevent frauds on the revenue. All such employments shall be reported to the Civil Service Commission. This amendment is in accordance with the views of the Secretary of the Treasury, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, and the Civil Service Commission. 
INTERNAL-REVENUE SERVICE. 
TEMPORARY EMPLOYMENT IN THE FOREST SERVICE. 
September 22, 1913. 
Paragraph 3, Subdivision IX, Schedule A, is hereby amended by substituting therefor the following: 
3. Guards and field assistants for reconnoissance parties employed temporarily during the season of danger from fires or when special work requires additions to the regular forest force. They shall serve only so long as absolutely required and in no case beyond the usual field season. So far as the commission may deem practicable such appointments shall be made from the registers of eligibles.
